prompt.context: Big Green Fuel Systems, a large provider of fuel additives required for the production of gasoline, has recently developed a substantially improved form of ethanol that adds 20% efficiency (measured as miles driven on a single gallon of ethanol). This version of fuel is costly to produce but the market is large and growing more rapidly as increased amounts of ethanol are being used in fuel blends. The company has engaged your team to help determine the viability of this new product, and, if it is viable, how to go about the process of launching it.
prompt.question: Determine the viability of Big Green Fuel Systems' new high-efficiency ethanol product and, if it is viable, recommend how to launch it.

clarifying_info.q: Is the company working in the US only?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, please concentrate on the US market only.

clarifying_info.q: Does the current infrastructure exist to make and support this product?
clarifying_info.a: It's compatible with other infrastructure in the external value chain, but Big Green does not yet have the capacity to mass produce it.

clarifying_info.q: What criteria does Big Green want us to use to determine the viability of the project?
What is the value chain for this product from Big Green to the consumer?
clarifying_info.a: Ethanol is delivered from manufacturers to fuel blenders, who then sell and deliver in bulk to filling stations, who in turn sell it to consumers.

clarifying_info.q: Does Big Green have a patent on this technology?

framework: Standard valuation: assess initial and recurring investment, incremental profit from the venture, and intangible benefits beyond ethanol sales (e.g., IP licensing, PR value).
Barriers and internal capability: identify barriers to launch, assess how the value chain will respond, and determine whether Big Green can manufacture at scale.
Standalone vs. licensing value: evaluate the product's worth to Big Green directly versus its value if sold or licensed to another producer.
Competitive response: anticipate what existing competitors will do and how that response ripples through the value chain.
Intangible benefits: consider positive PR, potential government incentives, spin-off opportunities, and positioning for future regulation.

questions.prompt: Size the US market for ethanol in gallons. You are given: total US miles driven last year = 1,800 billion miles; two blends exist — E-85 (85% ethanol, 10% of market) and E-15 (15% ethanol, 90% of market). Note: ignore the 20% efficiency improvement for this calculation.
questions.guidance: Candidate must recognize that average fuel economy (miles per gallon) is missing and proactively ask for it. Interviewer provides 20 mpg. Candidate should set up the formula: gallons of ethanol = (total miles / mpg) * ethanol content * market share, applied to each blend, then sum. After calculating, candidate should comment on the size of the market and ask about market fragmentation (answer: highly fragmented).

math.setup: Gallons of ethanol = [(1,800B miles / 20 mpg) * 85% * 10%] + [(1,800B miles / 20 mpg) * 15% * 90%]
steps: Total gallons of all fuel = 1,800B / 20 = 90B gallons
math.answer: ~19.8 billion gallons of ethanol per year

questions.prompt: The analysis has determined that there is no savings by using this new fuel blend — the fuel costs exactly as much to develop and deliver as can be gained by selling it. The CEO has staked his reputation on this product and is committed to delivering it. How would you best appeal to each level in the value chain to promote this improved product?
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through the value chain from manufacturer to consumer and identify a distinct value proposition at each level. Blenders: reduced blending volume needed (blend 20% less), competitive differentiation, reduced distribution costs, positioning for future government regulation. Filling stations: differentiation for eco-sensitive consumers, positive PR, appeals to drivers who want fewer fill-ups, reduced refill frequency from blenders lowers delivery costs, enables smaller-tank stations in new locations. Consumers: eco-friendliness, higher fuel cost offset by fewer fill-ups due to efficiency, time savings at the pump.

recommendation: Since the CEO has committed to rolling out the new fuel, the recommendation is to proceed with the launch, leveraging value-chain-specific messaging: appeal to blenders on reduced delivery costs and competitive positioning; appeal to filling stations on differentiation and PR; appeal to consumers on eco-friendliness and efficiency savings.
Support the launch with a pilot program to test efficacy and refine messaging before a gradual national roll-out.
risks: Price-perception problem: the higher cost to fill up may alienate consumers even though efficiency reduces total fill-ups over time.
Marketing costs to counter price-perception could erode margins.
Technical risk: the new fuel may be more corrosive than existing fuels, creating liability or infrastructure compatibility issues.
next_steps: Launch a regional pilot program, including targeted marketing efforts, to test the fuel's performance and consumer acceptance.
Apply lessons learned from the pilot to design a gradual national roll-out strategy.
Engage blenders and filling-station operators early to align on value propositions and logistics.
